“头一个试探就这样让了步，我怎能忍耐到底呢？”露西嚷道；心里带着几分渴望，想起忏悔的圣事，试着想一件自己能做的、最难受的事，好克苦肉身。倘若她的幽默感再活一点，露西或许会看出这题目的另一面；不过幽默——幸亏人间的情感能保持统一——多半是人生较晚的时节才发育的，露西这一场怒火，只是叫她更温柔、更宽容地想起普里基特巷那些泼妇。
留在楼下的三个人，各以各的方式被露西的怒火打动了。杰克·文特沃斯是个有幽默、有教养的人，觉得有趣，却仍恭敬，因为他到底还剩一点本领，能在亲眼见到绝对的纯洁时识得它。至于伍德豪斯，他又粗野地笑了一声，却不由得被慑住，不自觉地觉出自己是个多么寒酸的下作胚——露西那张苍白的脸里的轻蔑，给他的这一课，比几个钟头的讲理还要入骨。伍德豪斯小姐呢，她虽又急又慌，对争论中的问题却不是没有兴味。*她*对哥哥，对他能说的能做的一切，并不特别骇怕。他是她的汤姆——一个她一同玩儿过的男孩，他初次犯错时，她曾用尽做姐姐的全部力量护过他。她为他受的苦，远非露西所能受的，因此也就更能容他。她守住座位，圣女阿格尼丝靠在身后椅子里，怀着不安的镇定注视着事情的走向。她同露西一样不把钱放在心上；可是她禁不住想，倘若她能在“可怜的汤姆”身上促成一桩好事，将来有人指摘他时，也好替他顶一顶。伍德豪斯小姐年纪够大了，知道她的教区长不是理想英雄，只是个寻常人，他日后说不定真会时时拿“你那位哥哥，亲爱的”来作一篇劝世的教训。于是姐姐等着，心跳得快，等那个决定，一心巴望至少能记下一件慷慨的事，算到可怜的汤姆的好账上。

===Original===

“I think we are quite decided on the point,” said Jack Wentworth. “Knowing your sentiments, Wodehouse, I left directions with Waters about the papers. I think you will find him to be trusted, Miss Wodehouse, if you wish to consult him about letting or selling﻿—”
“By Jove!” exclaimed Wodehouse, under his breath.
“Which, I suppose,” continued the superb Jack, “you will wish to do under the pleasant circumstances, upon which I beg to offer you my congratulations. Now, Tom, my good fellow, I am at your service. I think we have done our business here.”
Wodehouse got up in his sulky reluctant way like a lazy dog. “I suppose you won’t try to move the furniture now?” he said. These were the only adieux he intended to make, and perhaps they might have been expressed with still less civility, had not Jack Wentworth been standing waiting for him at the door.
“Oh, Tom! I am so thankful you have done it!” cried Miss Wodehouse. “It is not that I care for the money; but oh, Tom, I am so glad to think nobody can say anything now.” She followed them wistfully to the door, not giving up hopes of a kinder parting. “I think it is very kind and nice of you, and what dear papa would have wished,” said the elder sister, forgetting how all her father’s plans had been brought to nothing; “and of course you will live here all the same?” she said, with a little eagerness, “that is, till﻿—till﻿—as long as we are here﻿—”
“Goodbye, Miss Wodehouse,” said Jack Wentworth. “I don’t think either your brother or I will stay much longer in Carlingford. You must accept my best wishes for your happiness all the same.”
“You are very kind, I am sure,” said the embarrassed bride; “and oh, Tom, you will surely say goodbye? Say goodbye once as if you meant it; don’t go away as if you did not care. Tom, I always was very fond of you; and don’t you feel a little different to us, now you’ve done us a kindness?” cried Miss Wodehouse, going out after him to the landing-place. But Wodehouse was in no humour to be gracious. Instead of paying any attention to her, he looked regretfully at the property he had lost.
“Goodbye,” he said, vaguely. “By Jove! I know better than Jack Wentworth does the value of property. We might have had a jolly month at Homburg out of that old place,” said the prodigal, with regret, as he went down the old-fashioned oak stair.

===Chinese===

“我想，这一点我们算是定妥了，”杰克·文特沃斯说。“知道你的心思，伍德豪斯，我已经就文书给沃特斯留了话。伍德豪斯小姐，你们若要商量出租或出售，我想你会发现他是靠得住的——”
“老天！”伍德豪斯低声惊呼。
“我想，在眼下这可喜的境况里——请容我道贺——你们是要出租或出售的，”气派超群的杰克接着说。“好了，汤姆，我的好伙计，听你吩咐。我们这里的事办完了。”
伍德豪斯懒狗似的，老大不情愿地站起来。“你们这会儿不搬家具了吧？”他说。这是他打算说的全部告别辞；若不是杰克·文特沃斯站在门口等他，说不定还会说得更不客气。
“哦，汤姆！你这样做了，我真感激！”伍德豪斯小姐嚷道。“倒不是我惦着钱；可是哦，汤姆，一想到如今谁也说不出什么了，我多高兴啊。”她怅怅地送他们到门口，还不死心，指望一场更亲热的道别。“你这样真是又好心又周到，也正是亲爱的爸爸生前的意思，”姐姐说，忘了父亲的全盘打算是怎么落空的；“当然，你们照样住在这儿？”她带着一点急切说，“就是说，住到——住到——我们在这儿多久，你们就——”
“再见了，伍德豪斯小姐，”杰克·文特沃斯说。“令兄同我，都不会在卡林福德久留了。还请容我向你的幸福致以最好的祝愿。”
“您真好，”这局促的新娘说；“哦，汤姆，你总要道个别吧？真心实意地告别一回；别这样满不在乎地走。汤姆，我一向顶喜欢你的；你帮了我们这个忙，如今心里对我们也不觉得两样一点吗？”伍德豪斯小姐一面嚷，一面追他到楼梯口。可伍德豪斯全无和颜悦色的兴致。他非但不理她，还惋惜地看着他失去的那份产业。
“再见，”他含含糊糊地说。“老天！产业值多少，我比杰克·文特沃斯明白。拿那处老宅子，本够我们去洪堡（Homburg）痛痛快快玩一个月的，”浪子一边惋惜着，一边走下那座老式橡木楼梯。

===Original===

That was his farewell to the house which he had entered so disastrously on the day of his father’s funeral. He followed his leader with a sulky aspect through the garden, not venturing to disobey, but yet feeling the weight of his chains. And this was how Wodehouse accomplished his personal share in the gift to his sisters, of which Miss Wodehouse told everybody that it was “so good of Tom!”

===Chinese===

这就是他给这所宅子留下的告别辞——父亲下葬那天，他那样闯祸地进了它的门。他阴沉沉地跟着他的首领穿过花园，不敢不从，却觉出锁链的分量。伍德豪斯给他妹妹们的那份馈赠里，他自己尽的一份力，就是这样；而伍德豪斯小姐逢人便说：“汤姆真是好得很！”

## XLIV / 四十四
===Original===

“Going to be married!” said the Squire; “and to a sister of﻿—I thought you told me she was as old as Dora, Frank? I did not expect to meet with any further complications,” the old man said, plaintively: “of course you know very well I don’t object to your marrying; but why on earth did you let me speak of Wentworth Rectory to Huxtable?” cried Mr. Wentworth. He was almost more impatient about this new variety in the family circumstances than he had been of more serious family distresses. “God bless me, sir,” said the Squire, “what do you mean by it? You take means to affront your aunts and lose Skelmersdale; and then you put it into my head to have Mary at Wentworth; and then you quarrel with the Rector, and get into hot water in Carlingford; and, to make an end of all, you coolly propose to an innocent young woman, and tell me you are going to marry﻿—what on earth do you mean?”
“I am going to marry some time, sir, I hope,” said the Perpetual Curate, with more cheerfulness than he felt; “but not at the present moment. Of course we both know that is impossible. I should like you to come with me and see her before you leave Carlingford. She would like it, and so should I.”
“Well, well,” said the Squire. Naturally, having been married so often himself, he could not refuse a certain response to such a call upon his sympathy. “I hope you have made a wise choice,” said the experienced father, not without a sigh; “a great deal depends upon that﻿—not only your own comfort, sir, but very often the character of your children and the credit of the family. You may laugh,” said Mr. Wentworth, to whom it was no laughing matter; “but long before you are as old as I am, you will know the truth of what I say. Your mother, Frank, was a specimen of what a woman ought to be﻿—not to speak of her own children, there was nobody else who ever knew how to manage Gerald and Jack. Of course I am not speaking of Mrs. Wentworth, who has her nursery to occupy her,” said the Squire, apologetically. “I hope you have made a judicious choice.”
“I hope so, too,” said Frank, who was somewhat amused by this view of the question﻿—“though I am not aware of having exercised any special choice in the matter,” he added, with a laugh. “However, I want you to come with me and see her, and then you will be able to judge for yourself.”

===Chinese===

“要结婚了！”老绅士说；“还是娶一位——的妹妹——我记得你跟我说过她有多拉那么大年纪，弗兰克？我没料到还会添新的麻烦，”老人委屈地说：“你成亲，我自然绝不反对，这你很清楚；可你到底为什么由着我对哈克斯托布尔提温特沃斯牧师宅？”文特沃斯先生叫道。家里情形这一新花样，几乎叫他比先前更严重的不幸还要不耐烦。“老天爷，先生，”老绅士说，“你到底是什么意思？你先是设法触怒姑妈，丢了斯凯尔默斯代尔；接着又撺掇我把玛丽弄回温特沃斯；然后同教区长吵架，在卡林福德惹一身麻烦；到头来，你又若无其事向一位无辜的年轻小姐求婚，告诉我你要结婚——你到底是什么意思？”
“我是打算将来什么时候结婚的，先生，我盼着，”常驻副牧师说，口气比心情轻快些；“眼下还不成。这不可能，咱们俩都清楚。我想请您在离开卡林福德之前，随我去见见她。她愿意，我也愿意。”
“好，好，”老绅士说。他自己结过那么多次婚，这样的恳求自然不能不答应几分。“盼着你挑得明智，”这位经验丰富的父亲说，不无叹息；“这上头关系大着呢——不光是你自己的舒坦，先生，还往往关系你儿女的品性、全家的体面。你尽管笑，”文特沃斯先生说——这在他可不是笑谈；“等你活到我这年纪，早晚会知道我的话不错。你母亲，弗兰克，就是女人应有的榜样——不提她自己的孩子，旁人里再没有谁管得住杰拉尔德和杰克。我自然不是说现在这位文特沃斯太太，她有她的育儿房要操心，”老绅士赔笑道。“盼着你挑得有眼光。”
“我也盼着，”弗兰克说，这个见地叫他暗自好笑——“虽说我不记得在这上头行使过什么特别的挑选，”他笑着补了一句。“不管怎样，我要您随我去见见她，您自己就能断定了。”

===Original===

The Squire shook his head, and looked as if he had travelled back into the heavy roll of family distresses. “I don’t mean to upbraid you, Frank,” he said﻿—“I daresay you have done what you thought was your duty﻿—but I think you might have taken a little pains to satisfy your aunt Leonora. You see what Gerald has made of it, with all his decorations and nonsense. That is a dreadful drawback with you clergymen. You fix your eyes so on one point that you get to think things important that are not in the least important. Could you imagine a man of the world like Jack﻿—he is not what I could wish, but still he is a man of the world,” said the Squire, who was capable of contradicting himself with perfect composure without knowing it. “Can you imagine *him* risking his prospects for a bit of external decoration? I don’t mind it myself,” said Mr. Wentworth, impartially﻿—“I don’t pretend to see, for my own part, why flowers at Easter should be considered more superstitious than holly at Christmas; but, bless my soul, sir, when your aunt thought so, what was the good of running right in her face for such a trifle? I never could understand you parsons,” the Squire said, with an impatient sigh﻿—“nobody, that I know of, ever considered me mercenary; but to ruin your own prospects, all for a trumpery bunch of flowers, and then to come and tell me you want to marry﻿—”
This was before luncheon, when Frank and his father were together in the dining-room waiting for the other members of the family, who began to arrive at this moment, and prevented any further discussion. After all, perhaps, it was a little ungenerous of the Squire to press his son so hard on the subject of those innocent Easter lilies, long ago withered, which certainly, looked at from this distance, did not appear important enough to sacrifice any prospects for. This was all the harder upon the unfortunate Curate, as even at the time his conviction of their necessity had not proved equal to the satisfactory settlement of the question. Miss Wentworth’s cook was an artiste so irreproachable that the luncheon provided was in itself perfect; but notwithstanding it was an uncomfortable meal.

===Chinese===

老绅士摇着头，那神气像是一头栽回了家庭烦恼的重重大浪里。“我不是要数落你，弗兰克，”他说——“你想必做的是你认为的本分——可你原可以稍稍费点心，把你莱奥诺拉姑妈敷衍好。你瞧杰拉尔德闹成什么样，满脑子装饰排场那一套。你们这些教士就有这个可怕的短处。眼睛死盯住一点，就把顶不要紧的东西盯成了要紧。你能想象杰克那样见过世面的人吗——他不如我愿，可他到底见过世面，”老绅士说，他能心平气和地自相矛盾而不自知。“你能想象他为一丁点外表的装饰去冒前程的风险？我自己倒不介意，”文特沃斯先生公道地说——“就我个人而言，我不明白复活节的鲜花何以比圣诞的冬青更迷信；可是，老天爷，先生，你姑妈既然那么想，为这么点鸡毛蒜皮迎面顶撞她，图什么？我永远弄不懂你们这些牧师，”老绅士不耐烦地叹道——“据我所知，从没有人说我贪财；可你们为一把破花毁了自己的前程，扭头又来告诉我你们要结婚——”
这是午饭前的事，弗兰克同父亲在饭厅里等着家里其他人，正这时他们到了，谈话就此打断。说起来，老绅士抓着那几枝清白无辜、早已枯萎的复活节百合，把儿子逼得这样紧，未免小气；隔着这段距离看，那几枝花实在不值得为它牺牲任何前程。这就更苦了倒霉的副牧师，因为即便当时，他对鲜花必要性的信念，也不曾把这问题圆满解决过。温特沃斯小姐的厨娘是位无懈可击的艺术家，那顿午饭本身十全十美；可它照旧吃得叫人不自在。

===Original===

Miss Leonora, in consequence of the contest going on in her own mind, was in an explosive and highly dangerous condition, not safe to be spoken to; and as for the Squire, he could not restrain the chance utterances of his impatience. Frank, who did his best to make himself agreeable as magnanimity required, had the mortification of hearing himself discussed in different tones of disapprobation while he ate his cold beef; for Mr. Wentworth’s broken sentences were not long of putting the party in possession of the new event, and the Perpetual Curate found himself the object of many wondering and pitying glances, in none of which could he read pure sympathy, much less congratulation. Even Gerald looked at him with a little elevation of his eyebrows, as if wondering how anybody could take the trouble to occupy his mind with such trifling temporal affairs as love and marriage. It was a wonderful relief to the unfortunate Curate when Miss Leonora had finished her glass of madeira, and rose from the table. He had no inclination to go upstairs, for his own part. “When you are ready, sir, you will find me in the garden,” he said to his father, who was to leave Carlingford next morning, and whom he had set his heart on taking to see Lucy. But his walk in the garden was far from being delightful to Frank. It even occurred to him, for a moment, that it would be a very good thing if a man could cut himself adrift from his relations at such a crisis of his life. After all, it was his own business﻿—the act most essentially personal of his entire existence; and then, with a little softening, he began to think of the girls at home﻿—of the little sister, who had a love-story of her own; and of Letty, who was Frank’s favourite, and had often confided to him the enthusiasm she would feel for his bride. “If she is nice,” Letty was in the habit of adding, “and of course she will be nice,”﻿—and at that thought the heart of the young lover escaped, and put forth its wings, and went off into that heaven of ideal excellence and beauty, more sweet, because more vague, than anything real, which stands instead of the old working-day skies and clouds at such a period of life.

莱奥诺拉小姐因为心里正斗着，处于一触即发、高度危险的状态，碰不得；至于老绅士，耐不住的性子时时漏出话来。弗兰克依照宽宏的要求极力周旋，却只得一边啃冷牛肉、一边听自己被人用不同的不满声调议论——文特沃斯先生的碎句子不久就叫全座知道了这件新事，常驻副牧师成了许多惊异怜悯目光的靶子，哪一束里也读不出纯然的同情，更谈不上道贺。连杰拉尔德也微微扬起眉毛看他，仿佛奇怪谁会费心去想恋爱结婚这类芝麻俗务。莱奥诺拉小姐喝完那杯马德拉酒、起身离席时，倒霉的副牧师才算大大松了口气。他自己无意上楼去。“您预备好了，先生，到园子里找我，”他对父亲说——老绅士明早就要离开卡林福德，弗兰克一心要带他去见露西。可他这趟园中散步，滋味远谈不上美妙。他甚至有一瞬想到，人在一生的这种关口，若能同亲戚一刀两断，倒也痛快。说到底，这是他自己的事——他一生中最纯属个人的一件事；随即心又软下来，想起家里的姑娘们——想起那位有着自己一段恋爱故事的小妹妹；还有莱蒂，她是弗兰克最疼的，常对他说，她会对他的新娘怀着怎样的热情。“要是她可爱的话，”莱蒂惯于补一句，“她当然会可爱的，”——想到这里，年轻恋人的心脱缰而出，张开翅膀，飞进那理想之至善至美的天堂——它比任何实在的东西都甜，就因为更朦胧——在人生的这段时期，它便顶替了往日劳碌的天空与云。

He had to drop down from a great height, and get rid in all haste of his celestial pinions, when he heard his aunt Dora calling him; and his self-command was not sufficient to conceal, as he obeyed that summons, a certain annoyed expression in his face.
“Frank,” said Miss Dora, coming softly after him with her handkerchief held over her head as a defence from the sun﻿—“oh, Frank, I want to speak to you. I couldn’t say anything at lunch because of everybody being there. If you would only stop a moment till I get my breath. Frank, my dear boy, I wish you joy. I do wish you joy with all my heart. I should so like just to go and kiss her, and tell her I shall love her for your sake.”
“You will soon love her for her own sake,” said Frank, to whom even this simple-minded sympathy was very grateful; “she is a great deal better than I am.”
“There is just one thing,” said Miss Dora. “Oh, Frank, my dear, you know I don’t pretend to be clever, like Leonora, or able to give you advice; but there *is* one thing. You know you have nothing to marry upon, and all has gone wrong. You are not to have Wentworth, and you are not to have Skelmersdale, and I think the family is going out of its senses not to see who is the most worthy. You have got nothing to live upon, my dear, dear boy!” said Miss Dora, withdrawing the handkerchief from her head in the excitement of the moment to apply it to her eyes.
“That is true enough,” said the Perpetual Curate; “but then we have not made up our minds that we must marry immediately﻿—”
“Frank,” said aunt Dora, with solemnity, breaking into his speech, “there is just *one* thing; and I can’t hold my tongue, though it may be very foolish, and they will all say it is my fault.” It was a very quiet summer-day, but still there was a faint rustle in the branches which alarmed the timid woman. She put her hand upon her nephew’s arm, and hastened him on to the little summerhouse in the wall, which was her special retirement. “Nobody ever comes here,” said Miss Dora; “they will never think of looking for us here.

“弗兰克，”多拉姑妈说，软软地跟在他身后，手绢搭在头上遮太阳——“哦，弗兰克，我有话同你说。吃午饭时人全，我没法开口。等我喘口气。弗兰克，好孩子，我祝你喜。我全心全意祝你喜。我真想这就去亲亲她，告诉她，看在你的份上我会疼她的。”

“有一件事，”多拉小姐说。“哦，弗兰克，亲爱的，你知道我不冒充莱奥诺拉那样聪明，也不敢给你出主意；可就是有一件事。你知道你们没有结婚的资本，一切都不顺。温特沃斯没了，斯凯尔默斯代尔也没了，我看这一家子是发了疯，竟看不出谁最配。你们没有糊口的东西，我亲爱的好孩子！”多拉小姐说着，激动之下，把遮阳的手绢从头上撤下来按到了眼睛上。
“这倒不假，”常驻副牧师说；“可我们也并没有拿定主意非马上结婚——”
“弗兰克，”多拉姑妈郑重地说，打断了他，“就是有一件事；我憋不住，兴许很傻，他们又会说是我的错。”那是个十分安静的夏日，可树叶间仍有一阵轻微的沙沙声，惊得这胆小的妇人变色。她把手搭在侄儿臂上，催他快走到墙边那座小凉亭去——那是她专用的退隐之地。“从来没有人到这儿来，”多拉小姐说；“他们绝想不到来这儿找我们。

===Original===

I am sure I never interfere with Leonora’s arrangements, nor take anything upon myself; but there is one thing, Frank﻿—”
“Yes,” said the Curate, “I understand what you mean: you are going to warn me about love in a cottage, and how foolish it would be to marry upon nothing; but, my dear aunt, we are not going to do anything rash; there is no such dreadful haste; don’t be agitated about it,” said the young man, with a smile. He was half amused and half irritated by the earnestness which almost took away the poor lady’s breath.
“You *don’t* know what I mean,” said aunt Dora. “Frank, you know very well I never interfere; but I can’t help being agitated when I see you on the brink of such a precipice. Oh, my dear boy, don’t be over-persuaded. There *is* one thing, and I must say it if I should die.” She had to pause a little to recover her voice, for haste and excitement had a tendency to make her inarticulate. “Frank,” said Miss Dora again, more solemnly than ever, “whatever you may be obliged to do﻿—though you were to write novels, or take pupils, or do translations﻿—oh, Frank, don’t look at me like that, as if I was going crazy. Whatever you may have to do, oh my dear, there is one thing﻿—don’t go and break people’s hearts, and put it off, and put it off, till it never happens!” cried the trembling little woman, with a sudden burst of tears. “Don’t say you can wait, for you can’t wait, and you oughtn’t to!” sobbed Miss Dora. She subsided altogether into her handkerchief and her chair as she uttered this startling and wholly unexpected piece of advice, and lay there in a little heap, all dissolving and floating away, overcome with her great effort, while her nephew stood looking at her from a height of astonishment almost too extreme for wondering. If the trees could have found a voice and counselled his immediate marriage, he could scarcely have been more surprised.
“You think I am losing my senses too,” said aunt Dora; “but that is because you don’t understand me. Oh Frank, my dear boy, there was once a time!﻿—perhaps everybody has forgotten it except me, but I have not forgotten it. They treated me like a baby, and Leonora had everything her own way. I don’t mean to say it was not for the best,” said the aggrieved woman.

我从不干预莱奥诺拉的主张，也从不揽事；可就是有一件事，弗兰克——”
“是，”副牧师说，“我明白您的意思：您要告诫我茅屋里的爱情，告诫我一无所有就结婚多么愚蠢；可是亲爱的姑妈，我们不打算莽撞行事；没有那么急迫；您别为这个激动，”年轻人微笑着说。老太太那份恳切，几乎叫她喘不上气，他看着半好笑、半烦躁。
“你不知道我的意思，”多拉姑妈说。“弗兰克，你知道我从不干预；可眼看你站在那样的悬崖边上，我没法不激动。哦，好孩子，别叫人劝得过了头。就是有一件事，我死也要说出来。”她不得不停一停缓嗓子，急切和激动常叫她说不成句。“弗兰克，”多拉小姐又说，比先前更郑重，“无论你将来不得不做什么——哪怕去写小说，去带学生，去做翻译——哦，弗兰克，别那样瞧我，仿佛我要疯了。无论你将来不得不做什么，哦亲爱的，有一件事——别去伤人家的心，一拖再拖，一拖再拖，拖到永远成不了！”发抖的小女人叫道，眼泪突然决了堤。“别说你等得起，你等不起，也不该等！”多拉小姐抽噎着说。她吐出这段惊世骇俗、全然出人意料的忠告，整个人缩进手绢和椅子里，瘫作一小堆，几乎消融飘散，为这番大费力而瘫软；她的侄儿立在一旁，从惊讶的高处俯视她，惊得连诧异都几乎装不下。倘若那些树开口劝他即刻完婚，他也不会更吃惊。
“你当我也失了心智，”多拉姑妈说；“可那是因为你不懂我。哦弗兰克，好孩子，从前也有一段时候！——兴许人人都忘了，只除了我，可我没有忘。他们把我当娃娃待，莱奥诺拉事事专断。我不是说那样不好，”委屈的女人说。

===Original===

“I know everything is for the best, if we could but see it: and perhaps Leonora was right when she said I never could have struggled with﻿—with a family, nor lived on a poor man’s income. My dear, it was before your uncle Charley died; and when we became rich, it﻿—didn’t matter,” said Miss Dora; “it was all over before then. Oh Frank! if I hadn’t experience I wouldn’t say a word. I don’t interfere about your opinions, like Leonora. There is just *one* thing,” cried the poor lady through her tears. Perhaps it was the recollection of the past which overcame Miss Dora, perhaps the force of habit which had made it natural for her to cry when she was much moved; but the fact is certain, that the Squire, when he came to the door of the summerhouse in search of Frank, found his sister weeping bitterly, and his son making efforts to console her, in which some sympathy was mingled with a certain half-amusement. Frank, like Lucy, felt tempted to laugh at the elderly romance; and yet his heart expanded warmly to his tender little foolish aunt, who, after all, might once have been young and in love like himself, though it was so odd to realise it. Mr. Wentworth, for his part, saw no humour whatever in the scene. He thought nothing less than that some fresh complication had taken place. Jack had committed some new enormity, or there was bad news from Charley in Malta, or unpleasant letters had come from home. “Bless my soul, sir, something new has happened,” said the Squire; and he was scarcely reassured, when Miss Dora stumbled up from her chair in great confusion, and wiped the tears from her eyes. He was suspicious of this meeting in the summerhouse, which seemed a quite unnecessary proceeding to Mr. Wentworth; and though he flattered himself he understood women, he could not give any reasonable explanation to himself of Dora’s tears.
“It is nothing﻿—nothing at all,” said Miss Dora: “it was not Frank’s doing in the least; he is always so considerate, and such a dear fellow. Thank you, my dear boy; my head is a little better; I think I will go in and lie down,” said the unlucky aunt. “You are not to mind me now, for I have quite got over my little attack; I always was so nervous,” said Miss Dora; “and I sometimes wonder whether it isn’t the Wentworth complaint coming on,” she added, with a natural female artifice which was not without its effect.

“我知道凡事都有天意，只是我们看不见罢了：莱奥诺拉说我无论如何斗不过——斗不过一大家子人、过不来穷日子，兴许她说得对。亲爱的，那是你查利叔叔去世以前的事；后来我们发了财，它——就无关紧要了，”多拉小姐说；“在那以前一切早已完了。哦弗兰克！我若不是有过切身经历，一个字也不会说。我不像莱奥诺拉那样干预你的见解。就是有一件事，”可怜的太太哭着说。压倒多拉小姐的，也许是旧事的回忆，也许是习惯的势力——她一动感情就哭，早已成了自然；可事实是确凿的：老绅士到凉亭门口来找弗兰克时，看见妹妹哭得伤心，儿子正竭力宽慰，那殷勤里一半是同情，一半是憋着的笑。弗兰克同露西一样，觉得这段老年的罗曼史有点好笑；可他的心又向着这位温柔的、小小的、痴心的姑妈暖暖张开——她到底也曾年轻过、恋爱过，同他自己一样，尽管这样想实在古怪。文特沃斯先生却全然看不出这一幕有什么幽默。他想得简单：又出了新的乱子。不是杰克闯了新的祸，就是马耳他的查利来了坏消息，要不就是家里来了不痛快的信。“老天爷，先生，出什么事了，”老绅士说；多拉小姐狼狈地从椅子上爬起来、擦去眼泪，他也未见得就放了心。他疑心这场凉亭密会——在他看来这全然多此一举；而且他虽自诩懂女人，却给多拉的眼泪找不出任何说得通的解释。
“没什么——没什么，”多拉小姐说；“一点不是弗兰克的不是；他向来那么体贴，那么可爱的孩子。谢谢你，好孩子；我头好些了；我想进去躺一躺，”倒霉的姑妈说。“这会儿你别管我了，我那点小发作已经全过去了；我一向神经弱，”多拉小姐说；“有时我不免疑心，是不是温特沃斯家的病上来了，”她补了一句——女人的这点天然心机，倒也不是全无效果。

===Original===

“I wish you would not talk nonsense,” said the Squire. “The Wentworth complaint is nothing to laugh at, but you are perfectly aware that it never attacks women.” Mr. Wentworth spoke with a little natural irritation, displeased to have his prerogative interfered with. When a man has all the suffering attendant upon a special complaint, it is hard not to have all the dignity. He felt so much and so justly annoyed by Miss Dora’s vain pretensions, that he forgot his anxiety about the secret conference in the summerhouse. “Women take such fantastic ideas into their heads,” he said to his son as they went away together. “Your aunt Dora is the kindest soul in the world; but now and then, sir, she is very absurd,” said the Squire. He could not get this presumptuous notion out of his head, but returned to it again and again, even after they had got into Grange Lane. “It has been in our family for two hundred years,” said Mr. Wentworth; “and I don’t think there is a single instance of its attacking a woman﻿—not even slightly, sir,” the Squire added, with irritation, as if Frank had taken the part of the female members of the family, which indeed the Curate had no thought of doing.
Miss Dora, for her part, having made this very successful diversion, escaped to the house, and to her own room, where she indulged in a headache all the afternoon, and certain tender recollections which were a wonderful resource at all times to the softhearted woman. “Oh, my dear boy, don’t be over-persuaded,” she had whispered into Frank’s ear as she left him; and her remonstrance, simple as it was, had no doubt produced a considerable effect upon the mind of the Perpetual Curate. He could not help thinking, as they emerged into the road, that it was chiefly the impatient and undutiful who secured their happiness. Those who were constant and patient, and able to deny themselves, instead of being rewarded for their higher qualities, were, on the contrary, put to the full test of the strength that was in them; while those who would not wait attained what they wanted, and on the whole, as to other matters, got on just as well as their stronger-minded neighbours.

===Chinese===

“盼你别胡说，”老绅士说。“温特沃斯家的病可不是闹着玩的，可你完全清楚，它从不袭击女人。”文特沃斯先生带着几分本能的恼怒说，特权被人染指，很不痛快。一种特殊的病，苦头既然全归男人受，威风若不能也全归男人，就太说不过去。多拉小姐那番虚妄的冒称叫他恼火又恼得有理，倒把凉亭密会引起的不安忘了。“女人的脑袋里就会钻进些古怪念头，”他同儿子一起走开时说。“你多拉姑妈是天底下心肠最好的人；可是先生，她时不时实在荒唐，”老绅士说。这个放肆的念头在他脑子里赶不出去，一遍又一遍翻上来，直到两人已走进格兰奇巷还没完。“这病在我们家传了两百年，”文特沃斯先生说；“我想不出有哪一例是女人染上的——一例也没有，先生，连轻的都没有，”老绅士恼火地补了一句，仿佛弗兰克偏袒了家里的女性——其实副牧师全无此意。
多拉小姐呢，这场调虎离山大获成功，脱身回屋，回到自己房里，痛痛快快头痛了一下午，又回味起那些温柔的旧事——它们对这心软的女人，向来是绝佳的慰藉。“哦，好孩子，别叫人劝得过了头，”她离开弗兰克时凑在他耳边低声说；她这番规劝虽简单，对常驻副牧师的心无疑起了相当的作用。走上大路时，他不由想：得着幸福的，多半倒是那些性急的、不孝的。坚贞的、有耐心的、能克己的人，非但得不到与高品质相称的报偿，反倒被推去经受力气的极限考验；不肯等的人却到手了所要的，而且在别的事情上，大体也同他们意志更坚强的邻人过得一样好。

===Original===

This germ of thought, it may be supposed, was stimulated into very warm life by the reflection that Lucy would have to leave Carlingford with her sister, without any definite prospect of returning again; and a certain flush of impatience came over the young man, not unnatural in the circumstances. It seemed to him that everybody else took their own way without waiting; and why should it be so certain that he alone, whose “way” implied harm to no one, should be the only man condemned to wait? Thus it will be seen that the “just one thing” insisted on by Miss Dora was far from being without effect on the mind of her nephew; upon whom, indeed, the events of the morning had wrought various changes of sentiment. When he walked up Grange Lane for the first time, it had been without any acknowledged intention of opening his mind to Lucy, and yet he had returned along the same prosaic and unsympathetic line of road her accepted lover; her accepted lover, triumphant in that fact, but without the least opening of any hope before him as to the conclusion of the engagement, which prudence had no hand in making. Now the footsteps of the Perpetual Curate fell firmly, not to say a little impatiently, upon the road over which he had carried so many varying thoughts. He was as penniless as ever, and as prospectless; but in the tossings of his natural impatience the young man had felt the reins hang loosely about his head, and knew that he was no more restrained than other men, but might, if he chose it, have his way like the rest of the world. It was true enough that he might have to pay for it after, as other people had done; but in the meantime the sense that he was his own master was sweet, and to have his will for once seemed no more than his right in the world. While these rebellious thoughts were going on in the Curate’s mind, his father, who suspected nothing, went steadily by his side, not without a little reluctance at the thought of the errand on which he was bound. “But they can’t marry for years, and nobody can tell what may happen in that time,” Mr. Wentworth said to himself, with the callousness of mature age, not suspecting the different ideas that were afloat in the mind of his son.

===Chinese===

不难设想，一想到露西将随姐姐离开卡林福德、归期茫茫，这颗思想的种子便发起了热；一股不耐的燥热涌上年轻人的心头，处此境地，原也自然。他觉得旁人个个说干就干，从不必等；凭什么偏偏他——他的“干法”又碍不着任何人——就该是唯一被判了等候的？由此可见，多拉小姐坚持的“就是一件事”，对她侄儿的心绝不是全无效果；的确，这一个上午的种种事变，已在他心里翻起好几重波澜。他头一回走上格兰奇巷时，本没有向露西剖白的成算，却沿着同一条索然无情的原路回来，成了她公认的恋人；成了公认的恋人，为这一事实扬扬得意，可这婚约的前途——它并非谨慎之功——却没有向他敞开一线指望。此刻，常驻副牧师的脚步落在路上，坚实，甚至带着点不耐——同一条路，他带着多少不同的心事走过。他还是身无分文，还是前程全无；可在他天性不耐的翻腾里，年轻人觉出缰绳松松地垂在头顶，知道自己并不比别人多受拘束，只要愿意，尽可以同世人一样自行其是。不错，事后他可能要付代价，旁人也付过；可眼下，自己做主的感觉是甜的，任性一回，似乎不过是他在这世上的本分权利。这些悖逆的念头在副牧师心里翻腾着，他的父亲毫无察觉，稳稳走在旁边，想着此行的差事，不无几分勉强。“反正他们几年内结不成婚，这几年里什么变故不会有，”文特沃斯先生自忖道，带着老年的冷漠，全不疑儿子心里正漂着另外的念头。

===Original===

Perhaps, on the whole, he was not sorry that Skelmersdale was destined otherwise, and that Huxtable had been spoken to about Wentworth Rectory; for, of course, Frank would have plunged into marriage at once if he had been possessed of anything to marry on; and it looked providential under the circumstances, as the Squire argued with himself privately, that at such a crisis the Perpetual Curate should have fallen between two stools of possible preferment, and should still be obliged to content himself with St. Roque’s. It was hard for Mr. Wentworth to reconcile himself to the idea that the wife of his favourite son should be the sister of —﻿—﻿—; for the Squire forgot that his own girls were Jack Wentworth’s sisters, and as such might be objected to in their turn by some other father. So the two gentlemen went to see Lucy, who was then in a very humble frame of mind, just recovered from her passion﻿—one of them rather congratulating himself on the obstacles which lay before the young couple, the other tossing his youthful head a little in the first impulses of self-will, feeling the reins lie loose upon him, and making up his mind to have his own way.

大体说来，斯凯尔默斯代尔既已另有归属、哈克斯托布尔又已被提起温特沃斯牧师宅，他也许倒不遗憾；因为弗兰克但凡有点结婚的资本，必定立刻一头扎进婚姻里去；老绅士私下里这样自辩：当此关口，常驻副牧师偏偏卡在两份可能的肥缺中间的空档里，仍只得安于圣罗克教堂，看着竟像天意。要文特沃斯先生咽下这口气实在难：他最疼爱的儿子的妻子，竟是——的姐姐；老绅士忘了自家的姑娘们也正是杰克的姐妹，轮到哪一位别的父亲，照样可以挑剔。两位绅士就这样去看露西——她那时心境极为谦卑，激情方过——一位暗自庆幸这对年轻人面前横着障碍，另一位凭着少年意气的头一阵任性，微微昂着头，觉出缰绳松松垂着，打定了主意要自行其是。

## XLV / 四十五
===Original===

While Mr. Frank Wentworth’s affairs were thus gathering to a crisis, other events likely to influence his fate were also taking place in Carlingford. Breakfast had been served a full half-hour later than usual in the Rectory, which had not improved the temper of the household. Everything was going on with the most wonderful quietness in that well-arranged house; but it was a quietness which would have made a sensitive visitor uncomfortable, and which woke horrible private qualms in the mind of the Rector. As for Mrs. Morgan, she fulfilled all her duties with a precision which was terrible to behold: instead of taking part in the conversation as usual, and having her own opinion, she had suddenly become possessed of such a spirit of meekness and acquiescence as filled her husband with dismay. The Rector was fond of his wife, and proud of her good sense, and her judgment, and powers of conversation. If she had been angry and found fault with him, he might have understood that mode of procedure; but as she was not angry, but only silent, the excellent man was terribly disconcerted, and could not tell what to do. He had done all he could to be conciliatory, and had already entered upon a great many explanations which had come to nothing for want of any response; and now she sat at the head of the table making tea with an imperturbable countenance, sometimes making little observations about the news, perfectly calm and dignified, but taking no part in anything more interesting, and turning off any reference that was made to her in the most skilful manner. “Mr. Morgan knows I never take any part in the gossip of Carlingford,” she said to Mr. Proctor, without any intention of wounding that good man; and he who had been in the midst of something about Mr. Wentworth came to an abrupt stop with the sense of having shown himself as a gossip, which was very injurious to his dignity. The late Rector, indeed, occupied a very uncomfortable position between the married people thus engaged in the absorbing excitement of their first quarrel. The quiet little arrows, which Mrs. Morgan intended only for her husband, grazed and stung him as they passed, without missing at the same time their intended aim; and he was the auditor, besides, of a great deal of information intended by the Rector for his wife’s benefit, to which Mrs. Morgan paid no manner of attention. 弗兰克·文特沃斯的事务这样一步步逼近危急关头的时候，卡林福德还有别的事情在进行，也多半要左右他的命运。教区长宅的早饭比平常足足晚了半个钟头，家中的脾气也不见好转。在那座安排得妥妥帖帖的宅子里，一切都进行得异常安静；可那是一种会叫敏感的客人浑身不自在的安静，它在教区长心里唤起了种种可怕的私下的疑惧。至于摩根太太，她把各项职分履行得一丝不苟，精确得吓人：她不再像往常那样加入谈话、发表己见，而是突然被一种温顺与默许的灵附了体，把她丈夫吓得不轻。教区长爱他的太太，也为她的见识、她的判断力和谈吐的本领自豪。她若是动了气、数落他，那种程序他还懂得应付；可她并不动气，只是沉默，这位好人便狼狈到了极点，不知如何是好。他百般讨好，已经起了好几回头，讲了一大篇一大篇的解释，都因为没人接话而落了空；此刻她坐在桌上首斟茶，神色不动，偶尔对新闻发表一两句小评论，平静极了，体面极了，但稍微有意思一点的事一概不沾边，谁把话头递到她跟前，都被她用最巧妙的手法挡开。“摩根先生知道，我从不参与卡林福德的闲话，”她对普罗克特先生说，并没有伤这位好人的意思；他正讲到文特沃斯先生的半当腰，猛地刹住，只觉自己俨然成了个搬弄是非的人，大大有损他的尊严。这位前任教区长夹在中间，实在处境尴尬——这对夫妇正沉在头一场争吵的全神贯注的兴奋里。摩根太太那些只对她丈夫放的小小暗箭，擦着普罗克特先生飞过，扎他一下，同时却也不曾错过它们的目标；此外，教区长说给太太听训诲的大量话语，也全数落进他的耳朵，摩根太太一概不理。普

Proctor was not a man of very lively observation, but he could not quite shut his eyes to the position of affairs; and the natural effect upon his mind, in the circumstances, was to turn his thoughts towards his mild Mary, whom he did not quite recognise as yet under her Christian name. He called her Miss Wodehouse in his heart even while in the act of making comparisons very unfavourable to the Rector’s wife, and then he introduced benevolently the subject of his new rectory, which surely must be safe ground.
“It is a pretty little place,” Mr. Proctor said, with satisfaction: “of course it is but a small living compared to Carlingford. I hope you will come and see me, after﻿—it is furnished,” said the bashful bridegroom: “it is a nuisance to have all that to look after for one’s self﻿—”
“I hope you will have somebody to help you,” said Mrs. Morgan, with a little earnestness; “gentlemen don’t understand about such things. When you have one piece of furniture in bad taste, it spoils a whole room﻿—carpets, for instance﻿—” said the Rector’s wife. She looked at Mr. Proctor so severely that the good man faltered, though he was not aware of the full extent of his guiltiness.
“I am sure I don’t know,” he said: “I told the man here to provide everything as it ought to be; and I think we were very successful,” continued Mr. Proctor, with a little complacency: to be sure, they were in the dining-room at the moment, being still at the breakfast-table. “Buller knows a great deal about that sort of thing, but then he is too ecclesiological for my taste. I like things to look cheerful,” said the unsuspicious man. “Buller is the only man that could be reckoned on if any living were to fall vacant. It is very odd nowadays how indifferent men are about the Church. I don’t say that it is not very pleasant at All Souls; but a house of one’s own, you know﻿—” said Mr. Proctor, looking with a little awkward enthusiasm at his recently-married brother; “of course I mean a sphere﻿—a career﻿—”
“Oh, ah, yes,” said Mr. Morgan, with momentary gruffness; “but everything has its drawbacks. I don’t think Buller would take a living. He knows too well what’s comfortable,” said the suffering man. “The next living that falls will have to go to someone out of the college,” said Mr. Morgan. He spoke with a tone of importance and significance which moved Mr.

“那是处可爱的小地方，”普罗克特先生满意地说：“比起卡林福德来，圣俸当然算小。我希望你们来看看我，等——家具是齐的，”这羞怯的新郎说：“这一应事情都要自己操心，实在烦人——”
“但愿有人帮帮你，”摩根太太带着一点恳切说；“先生们不懂这一套。一件家具趣味一坏，就毁了一整间屋子——比如地毯——”教区长的太太说。她那样严厉地看着普罗克特先生，好人讷讷起来，虽则他还不清楚自己罪孽的全部轻重。
“我说不好，”他说：“我吩咐这里的人，样样照规矩置办；我看我们办得很成功，”普罗克特先生接着说，带一点自得：的确，此刻他们正在饭厅里，还坐在早餐桌前呢。“布勒（Buller）对那一套懂得很多，只是他太教会学究气，不合我的口味。我喜欢屋子看着喜气，”这没有机心的人说。“哪个圣俸一空出来，靠得住顶得上的，只有布勒。如今的人对教会这样冷淡，真是怪事。我不是说万灵学院不舒服；可自己的宅子，你知道——”普罗克特先生说着，带着一点局促的热望，望了望他那位新婚的内弟；“当然我是说一片天地——一番前程——”

Proctor, though he was not rapid in his perceptions, to look across at him for further information.
“Most people have some crotchet or other,” said the Rector. “When a man’s views are clear about subscription, and that sort of thing, he generally goes as far wrong the other way. Buller might go out to Central Africa, perhaps, if there was a bishopric of Wahuma﻿—or what is the name, my dear, in that Nile book?”
“I have not read it,” said Mrs. Morgan, and she made no further remark.
Thus discouraged in his little attempt at amity, the Rector resumed after a moment, “Wentworth’s brother has sent in his resignation to his bishop. There is no doubt about it any longer. I thought that delusion had been over, at all events; and I suppose now Wentworth will be provided for,” said Mr. Morgan, not without a little anxiety.
“No; they are all equally crotchety, I think,” said Mr. Proctor. “I know about them, through my﻿—my connection with the Wodehouses, you know. I should not wonder, for my own part, if he went after his brother, who is a very intelligent man, though mistaken,” the late Rector added, with respect. “As for Frank Wentworth, he is a little hotheaded. I had a long conversation the other night with the elder brother. I tried to draw him out about Burgon’s book, but he declined to enter into the question. Frank has made up his mind to stay in Carlingford. I understand he thinks it right on account of his character being called in question here; though, of course, no one in his senses could have had any doubt how *that* would turn out,” said Mr. Proctor, forgetting that he himself had been very doubtful about the Curate. “From what I hear, they are all very crotchety,” he continued, and finished his breakfast calmly, as if that settled the question. As for Mrs. Morgan, even this interesting statement had no effect upon her. She looked up suddenly at one moment as if intending to dart a reproachful glance at her husband, but bethought herself in time, and remained passive as before; not the less, however, was she moved by what she had just heard. It was not Mr. Wentworth she was thinking of, except in a very secondary degree. What occupied her, and made her reflections bitter, was the thought that her husband﻿—the man to whom she had been faithful for ten weary years﻿—had taken himself down off the pedestal on which she had placed him.

克特先生的心——他虽然领会得慢，也掉过头去望着他，等下文。
“人大都有个把怪癖，”教区长说。“一个人在签署认信那一类问题上见解一清楚，多半又朝另一头错出一样远。布勒也许会去中非，倘若有一个瓦胡马（Wahuma）主教区的话——亲爱的，那本讲尼罗河的书里叫什么来着？”
“我没读过，”摩根太太说，再没有别的话。
这番修好的小小尝试碰了壁，教区长顿了一顿，重新开口：“文特沃斯的弟弟已把辞呈递给他的主教了。这一点再没有疑问了。我原想那场痴迷总算是过去了；如今文特沃斯想必会得到安置，”摩根先生说，不无一点焦灼。
“不；我看他们个个一样地怪，”普罗克特先生说。“他们家的事我知道，因为——因为我同伍德豪斯家的亲，你知道。要叫我说，说不定他会跟着他弟弟走，那是个非常聪明的人，虽说错了路，”前任教区长怀着敬意补上一句。“至于弗兰克·文特沃斯，他是个小火性。前几天晚上我同他哥哥谈了很久。我想引他谈谈伯贡（Burgon）那本书，他不肯接这个茬。弗兰克拿定主意留在卡林福德了。我了解，他认为自己的名誉在这里受了指摘，留下来才算对；虽说*那*件事会怎样了结，头脑清楚的人当然谁都不曾怀疑过，”普罗克特先生说，忘了他自己就曾对副牧师满肚子疑虑。“据我听来，他们一家个个都怪，”他接着说，安安稳稳吃完了早饭，仿佛这一句便断结了全案。至于摩根太太，连这样有趣的话也没有打动她。有一刻她猛地抬起头，仿佛要朝她丈夫投去一道责备的眼色，好在及时醒悟，依旧消极如前；可她方才听到的话，并不因此就不曾打动她。她心里想的不是文特沃斯先生——至多在其次。占据她、叫她的反思发苦的，是这样一个念头：她的丈夫——她苦守了十年的那个人——自己从她给他筑的座上走下来了。

===Original===

“To make idols, and to find them clay,” she said plaintively in her own mind. Women were all fools to spend their time and strength in constructing such pedestals, Mrs. Morgan thought to herself with bitterness; and as to the men who were so perpetually dethroning themselves, how were they to be designated? To think of her William, of whom she had once made a hero, ruining thus, for a little petty malice and rivalry, the prospects of another man! While these painful reflections were going through her mind, she was putting away her tea-caddy, and preparing to leave the gentlemen to their own affairs. “We shall see you at dinner at six,” she said, with a constrained little smile, to Mr. Proctor, and went upstairs with her key-basket in her hand without taking any special notice of the Rector. Mr. Leeson was to come to dinner that day legitimately by invitation, and Mrs. Morgan, who felt it would be a little consolation to disappoint the hungry Curate for once, was making up her mind, as she went upstairs, not to have the All Souls pudding, of which he showed so high an appreciation. It almost seemed to her as if this spark of ill-nature was receiving a summary chastisement, when she heard steps ascending behind her. Mrs. Morgan objected to have men lounging about her drawing-room in the morning. She thought Mr. Proctor was coming to bestow a little more of his confidence upon her, and perhaps to consult her about his furnishing; and being occupied by her own troubles, she had no patience for a tiresome, middle-aged lover, who no doubt was going to disappoint and disenchant another woman. She sat down, accordingly, with a sigh of impatience at her worktable, turning her back to the door. Perhaps, when he saw her inhospitable attitude, he might go away and not bother her. And Mrs. Morgan took out some stockings to darn, as being a discontented occupation, and was considering within herself what simple preparation she could have instead of the All Souls pudding, when, looking up suddenly, she saw, not Mr. Proctor, but the Rector, standing looking down upon her within a few steps of her chair. When she perceived him, it was not in nature to refrain from certain symptoms of agitation.

“造一尊偶像，末了发现它是泥胎，”她在心里凄凄地自语。女人全是傻子，把光阴气力花在筑这样的高座上，摩根太太苦涩地自忖；至于那些不断自己把自己掀下宝座的男人，又该叫他们什么呢？想想她的威廉——她曾把他造成一位英雄——竟为一点小小的恶意和争胜，这样毁了另一个人的前程！这些痛楚的念头在心头过了一遍，她正收起茶叶罐，预备撇下先生们去办他们自己的事。“晚饭六点，我们恭候，”她对普罗克特先生说着，勉强一笑，提着钥匙篮上楼去了，对教区长未加特别的理会。利森先生那天是正经受了请来吃饭的；摩根太太心想，叫这位馋嘴的副牧师失望一回，也算一点安慰，一面上楼，一面打定主意不做那道万灵学院布丁——他对它的赏识是出了名的高。她觉得这一星坏心眼仿佛立刻遭了现世报：她听见身后有脚步声跟上来。摩根太太反对男人上午在她客厅里游荡。她当是普罗克特先生又来倾吐他的体己，或许还要请她参谋家具；她正被自己的烦恼占着，对一位腻人的中年情人全无耐性——此人无疑又要去叫另一个女人失望、幻灭。于是她在活计桌前坐下，不耐地叹了口气，背朝着门。他见了这副不客气的姿态，或许就走了，不来搅她。摩根太太拿出几双长袜来织补——算是顶没好气的一种活计——一面盘算着拿什么家常预备顶替那道万灵学院布丁；忽然一抬头，站在她椅子几步之内、俯视着她的，不是普罗克特先生，而是教区长。她一看见他，天性拦不住那几阵激动。

===Original===

The thoughts she had been indulging in brought suddenly a rush of guilty colour to her face; but she commanded herself as well as she could, and went on darning her stockings, with her heart beating very loud in her breast.
“My dear,” said the Rector, taking a seat near her, “I don’t know what it is that has risen between us. We look as if we had quarrelled; and I thought we had made up our minds never to quarrel.” The words were rather soft in their signification, but Mr. Morgan could not help speaking severely, as was natural to his voice; which was perhaps, in the present case, all the better for his wife.
“I don’t know what you may consider quarrelling, William,” said Mrs. Morgan, “but I am sure I have never made any complaint.”
“No,” said the Rector; “I have seen women do that before. You don’t make any complaint, but you look as if you disapproved of everything. I feel it all the more just now because I want to consult you; and, after all, the occasion was no such﻿—”
“I never said there was any occasion. I am sure I never made any complaint. You said you wanted to consult me, William?” Mrs. Morgan went on darning her stockings while she was speaking, and the Rector, like most other men, objected to be spoken to by the lips only. He would have liked to toss the stocking out of the window, though it was his own, and the task of repairing it was one of a devoted wife’s first duties, according to the code of female proprieties in which both the husband and wife had been brought up.
“Yes,” said the Rector, with a sigh. “The truth is, I have just got a letter from Harry Scarsfield, who was my pet pupil long ago. He tells me my father’s old rectory is vacant, where we were all brought up. There used to be a constant intercourse between the Hall and the Rectory when I was a lad. They are very nice people the Scarsfields﻿—at least they used to be very nice people; and Harry has his mother living with him, and the family has never been broken up, I believe. We used to know everybody about there,” said Mr. Morgan, abandoning himself to recollections in a manner most mysterious to his wife. “There is the letter, my dear,” and he put it down upon her table, and began to play with the reels of cotton in her workbox unconsciously, as he had not done for a long time; which, unawares to herself, had a softening influence upon Mrs. Morgan’s heart.

===Chinese===

方才沉溺的那些念头，蓦地涌上一股心虚的红；可她竭力镇住自己，只管织补长袜，心口擂鼓一样地跳。
“亲爱的，”教区长在她近旁坐下说，“我不知道咱们中间起了什么。咱们这模样像是拌了嘴；我还当我们拿定主意永远不拌嘴呢。”这话的意思原是软的，可摩根先生天生那副嗓音，说起话来不由自主地严厉——在这桩事上，对他太太或许倒全然是好事。
“你眼里的拌嘴是什么，我不知道，威廉，”摩根太太说，“可我担保我从没有抱怨过一句。”
“是没有，”教区长说；“这种把戏我从前见过。你不抱怨，可你那副神色，样样都不以为然。我此刻尤其感觉到这一点，因为我要同你商量；再说，那桩事也未必那样——”
“我从没说过有什么事。我担保我从没有抱怨过。你是说，你要同我商量，威廉？”摩根太太一面说，一面只管织补；教区长同大多数男人一样，不乐意人家只用嘴唇同他讲话。他真想把那只长袜扔出窗外去——虽说那是他自己的袜子，织补它又是贤妻的头一样本分，按夫妇俩从小受的那套女诫规矩。
“是这么回事，”教区长叹了口气说。“我刚收到哈里·斯卡斯菲尔德（Harry Scarsfield）一封信，他从前是我得意的门生。他告诉我，我父亲的老教区长宅空出来了——我们弟兄都是在那儿长大的。我做孩子的时候，庄园和牧师宅之间来往不断。斯卡斯菲尔德一家都是好人——至少从前是很好的人；哈里同他母亲住在一起，那一家人从来没有散过，我想。那一带我们从前谁都认得，”摩根先生说，一任自己沉进回忆里，那副模样在他太太看来神秘极了。“信在这儿，亲爱的，”他把信放在她桌上，不自觉地摆弄起她针线盒里的线轴来——他好久没有这样了；摩根太太的心不知不觉给这一下软化了。

“I do not know anything about the Scarsfields,” she said, without taking up the letter, “and I cannot see what you have to do with this. Does he wish you to recommend someone?” Mrs. Morgan added, with a momentary interest; for she had, of course, like other people, a relation in a poor living, whom it would have been satisfactory to recommend.
“He says I may have it if I have a mind,” said the Rector curtly, betraying a little aggravation in his tone.
“You, William?” said Mrs. Morgan. She was so much surprised that she laid down her stocking and looked him straight in the face, which she had not done for many days; and it was wonderful how hard she found it to keep up her reserve, after having once looked her husband in the eyes. “But it is not much more than six months since you were settled in Carlingford,” she said, still lost in amazement. “You cannot possibly mean to make a change so soon? and then the difference of the position,” said the Rector’s wife. As she looked at him, she became more and more aware of some meaning in his face which she did not understand; and more and more, as it became necessary to understand him, the reserves and self-defences of the first quarrel gave way and dispersed. “I don’t think I quite know what you mean,” she said, faltering a little. “I don’t understand why you should think of a change.”
“A good country living is a very good position,” said the Rector; “it is not nearly so troublesome as a town like Carlingford. There is no Dissent that I know of, and no﻿—” (here Mr. Morgan paused for a moment, not knowing what word to use)﻿—“no disturbing influences: of course I would not take such a step without your concurrence, my dear,” the Rector continued; and then there followed a bewildering pause. Mrs. Morgan’s first sensation after the astonishment with which she heard this strange proposal was mortification﻿—the vivid shame and vexation of a woman when she is obliged to own to herself that her husband has been worsted, and is retiring from the field.
“If you think it right﻿—if you think it best﻿—of course I can have nothing to say,” said the Rector’s wife; and she took up her stocking with a stinging sense of discomfiture. She had meant that her husband should be the first man in Carlingford﻿—that he should gain everybody’s respect and veneration, and become the ideal parish-priest of that favourite and fortunate place.

“斯卡斯菲尔德家的事我一样不知道，”她说，没有去拿那封信，“我也不明白这同你有什么相干。他是要你荐人吗？”摩根太太一时来了兴致；因为她自然同旁人一样，也有一位领着穷圣俸的亲戚，能荐一个岂不称心。
“他说，我若有意，这圣俸便是我的，”教区长简短地说，口气里透出一点恼意。
“你，威廉？”摩根太太说。她吃惊到这般地步，竟放下长袜，直直望着他的脸——多少天来这是头一回；而一经同丈夫对视，要保持那份矜持竟这样难，真是出奇。“可你到卡林福德安顿下来，还不满六个月呢，”她说，还怔在惊异里。“你总不至于这么快就想换？再说地位的悬殊，”教区长的太太说。她望着他，愈发觉出他脸上有一种她不懂的深意；而愈是需要懂得他时，头一场口角筑下的堤防和自卫，便愈发溃散了。“我怕我还不大明白你的意思，”她略略讷讷地说。“我不明白你为什么想到换地方。”
“一处好的乡间圣俸是个很好的位置，”教区长说；“绝不似卡林福德这样的市镇烦人。据我所知那里没有不奉国教的，也没有——”（摩根先生在此顿住，一时不知用什么字眼）“——没有搅扰的因素：当然，亲爱的，没有你的首肯，这样一步我是不会走的，”教区长接着说；随后是一阵令人惶惑的沉默。摩根太太听罢这个古怪提议，惊奇过后头一阵感觉是羞恼——一个女人不得不自认丈夫败下阵去、正要退出战场时，那种刺心的羞愤。
“你若觉得对——你若觉得最好——我自然无可再说，”教区长的太太说；她拾起长袜，带着一股扎心的失意。她原指望丈夫做卡林福德的第一人——赢得人人敬重，成为那块人杰地灵的宝地上的理想教区司铎。

===Original===

Every kind of good work and benevolent undertaking was to be connected with his name, according to the visions which Mrs. Morgan had framed when she came first to Carlingford, not without such a participation on her own part as should entitle her to the milder glory appertaining to the good Rector’s wife. All these hopes were now to be blotted out ignominiously. Defeat and retreat and failure were to be the conclusion of their first essay at life. “You are the best judge of what you ought to do,” she said, with as much calmness as she could muster, but she could have dropped bitter tears upon the stocking she was mending if that would have done any good.
“I will do nothing without your consent,” said the Rector. “Young Wentworth is going to stay in Carlingford. You need not look up so sharply, as if you were vexed to think *that* had anything to do with it. If he had not behaved like a fool, I never could have been led into such a mistake,” said Mr. Morgan, with indignation, taking a little walk to the other end of the room to refresh himself. “At the same time,” said the Rector, severely, coming back after a pause, “to show any ill-feeling would be very unchristian either on your side or mine. If I were to accept Harry Scarsfield’s offer, Proctor and I would do all we could to have young Wentworth appointed to Carlingford. There is nobody just now at All Souls to take the living; and however much you may disapprove of him, my dear,” said Mr. Morgan, with increasing severity, “there is nothing that I know to be said against him as a clergyman. If you can make up your mind to consent to it, and can see affairs in the same light as they appear to me, that is what I intend to do﻿—”
Mrs. Morgan’s stocking had dropped on her knees as she listened; then it dropped on the floor, and she took no notice of it. When the Rector had finally delivered himself of his sentiments, which he did in the voice of a judge who was condemning some unfortunate to the utmost penalties of the law, his wife marked the conclusion of the sentence by a sob of strange excitement. She kept gazing at him for a few moments without feeling able to speak, and then she put down her face into her hands. Words were too feeble to give utterance to her feelings at such a supreme moment.

===Chinese===

一切善工、一切慈善的事业，都该同他的名字连在一起——按摩根太太初来卡林福德时织就的图景，她自己也少不得要在里面有一份，配得上好教区长太太那份次一等的光荣。这一切指望，如今都要不体面地一笔勾销。败退、溃走、失利，要成为他们人生头一役的结局。“怎样做合适，你比谁都清楚，”她尽其所能地平静说；可若真有半点用处，她真能把苦泪滴在那只织补的长袜上。
“没有你的同意，我什么都不做，”教区长说。“小文特沃斯要留在卡林福德了。你不必那样锐利地抬头，好像一想到*那*件事与此有关就恼。他若不是行事像个傻子，我也决不会被引到那样的错处，”摩根先生愤愤地说，在屋里踱到那头去定一定神。“不过同时，”教区长停了停，严峻地走回来说，“不论你是我这边，心存一点恶感，都不是基督徒所当为。我若接受哈里·斯卡斯菲尔德的提议，普罗克特同我就会尽力设法，保小文特沃斯补卡林福德的缺。眼下万灵学院里没有别人可以来领这圣俸；而且，亲爱的，不管你怎样看不惯他，”摩根先生愈发严厉地说，“就我所知，作为一个教士，他没有一处可以说嘴的。你若能定下心同意这件事，能同我一样看待这局面，这便是我的打算——”
摩根太太听着，长袜先是落在膝上；随后落在地板上，她也不理会。教区长终于发表完他的意见——用的是法官给不幸的人判满刑的腔调——他的太太用一声异样激动的呜咽，标出了判决的句读。她凝望着他，好一阵说不出话，随后把脸埋进双手里。在这样一个至高的时刻，言语太贫弱，装不下她的感情。

===Original===

“Oh, William, I wonder if you can ever forgive me,” sobbed the Rector’s wife, with a depth of compunction which he, good man, was totally unprepared to meet, and knew no occasion for. He was even at the moment a little puzzled to have such a despairing petition addressed to him. “I hope so, my dear,” he said, very sedately, as he came and sat down beside her, and could not refrain from uttering a little lecture upon temper, which fortunately Mrs. Morgan was too much excited to pay any attention to. “It would be a great deal better if you did not give way to your feelings,” said the Rector; “but in the meantime, my dear, it is your advice I want, for we must not take such a step unadvisedly,” and he lifted up the stocking that had fallen, and contemplated, not without surprise, the emotion of his wife. The excellent man was as entirely unconscious that he was being put up again at that moment with acclamations upon his pedestal, as that he had at a former time been violently displaced from it, and thrown into the category of broken idols. All this would have been as Sanskrit to the Rector of Carlingford; and the only resource he had was to make in his own mind certain half-pitying, half-affectionate remarks upon the inexplicable weakness of women, and to pick up the stocking which his wife was darning, and finally to stroke her hair, which was still as pretty and soft and brown as it had been ten years ago. Under such circumstances a man does not object to feel himself on a platform of moral superiority. He even began to pet her a little, with a pleasant sense of forgiveness and forbearance. “You were perhaps a little cross, my love, but you don’t think I am the man to be hard upon you,” said the Rector. “Now you must dry your eyes and give me your advice﻿—you know how much confidence I have always had in your advice﻿—”
“Forgive me, William. I don’t think there is anyone so good as you are; and as long as we are together it does not matter to me where we are,” said the repentant woman. But as she lifted up her head, her eye fell on the carpet, and a gleam of sudden delight passed through Mrs. Morgan’s mind.

===Chinese===

“哦，威廉，不知你能不能饶恕我，”教区长的太太抽泣道，那份悔愧的深重，好人全然不曾防备，也全然不知来由。那一刻他甚至有点纳闷，这样绝望的一纸请求怎么会递到他面前来。“但愿能，亲爱的，”他郑重地说，走过去坐在她身旁，忍不住还就脾气发了一篇小训诫——所幸摩根太太激动得一句也没听进去。“你要是不任着性子，就好多啦，”教区长说；“不过眼下，亲爱的，我要的是你的主意，这样一步不可轻率，”他拾起掉落的长袜，不无惊异地端详着太太的激动。这位好人全然不觉，此刻他正被欢呼声重新举上他的宝座，正如从前他全然不觉自己曾被粗暴地掀下来，归入破偶像一类。这一切，对卡林福德的教区长来说，都会像梵文一样难解；他唯一的办法，是在心里对女人这种不可解的软弱发几句半怜半爱的感想，拾起太太织补的那只长袜，末了抚一抚她的头发——十年前怎样柔滑好看的一头棕发，如今还怎样柔滑好看。在这样的情形下，一个男人不反对自觉站在道德的优台上。他甚至带着愉快宽宥、优容的心肠，怜爱起她来。“你兴许有一点点小性儿，我的宝贝，可你不至于想我是苛待你的人，”教区长说。“现在你得擦干眼睛，给我出主意——你知道我一向多信你的主意——”
“饶恕我，威廉。我想再没有人像你这样好；只要我们在一起，我们在哪儿都不要紧，”这悔罪的女人说。可她一抬头，眼睛落在地毯上，一道突来的欢喜闪过摩根太太的心头。

===Original===

To be delivered from all her suspicions and injurious thoughts about her husband would have been a deliverance great enough for one day; but at the same happy moment to see a means of deliverance from the smaller as well as the greater cross of her existence seemed almost too good to be credible. She brightened up immediately when that thought occurred to her. “I think it is the very best thing you could do,” she said. “We are both so fond of the country, and it is so much nicer to manage a country parish than a town one. We might have lived all our lives in Carlingford without knowing above half of the poor people,” said Mrs. Morgan, growing in warmth as she went on; “it is so different in a country parish. I never liked to say anything,” she continued, with subtle feminine policy, “but I never﻿—much﻿—cared for Carlingford.” She gave a sigh as she spoke, for she thought of the Virginian creeper and the five feet of new wall at that side of the garden, which had just been completed, to shut out the view of the train. Life does not contain any perfect pleasure. But when Mrs. Morgan stooped to lift up some stray reels of cotton which the Rector’s clumsy fingers had dropped out of her workbox, her eye was again attracted by the gigantic roses and tulips on the carpet, and content and satisfaction filled her heart.
“I have felt the same thing, my dear,” said Mr. Morgan. “I don’t say anything against Mr. Finial as an architect, but Scott himself could make nothing of such a hideous church. I don’t suppose Wentworth will mind,” said the Rector, with a curious sense of superiority. He felt his own magnanimous conduct at the moment almost as much as his wife had done, and could not help regarding Carlingford Church as the gift-horse which was not to be examined too closely in the mouth.
“No,” said Mrs. Morgan, not without a passing sensation of doubt on this point; “if he had only been frank and explained everything, there never could have been any mistake; but I am glad it has all happened,” said the Rector’s wife, with a little enthusiasm. “Oh, William, I have been such a wretch﻿—I have been thinking﻿—but now you are heaping coals of fire on his head,” she cried, with a hysterical sound in her throat. It was no matter to her that she herself scarcely knew what she meant, and that the good Rector had not the faintest understanding of it.

===Chinese===

从她对丈夫的一切猜疑、一切刻薄的念头里解脱出来，这一天得的解脱本来已经够大了；偏偏又在同一个幸福的时刻，看见一条出路，把她生活里小一点的、大一点的十字架一并解脱，这几乎好得叫人不敢信。这念头一闪，她立刻明朗起来。“我看这是你顶好的一步，”她说。“咱们俩都这样爱乡下；管一个乡间教区，又比管一个市镇教区惬意得多。在卡林福德住一辈子，穷人我们也认不得一半，”摩根太太愈说愈热；“乡间教区就两样了。我一直不好说出口，”她带着女性精微的心计接着说，“可是我从来不——大——喜欢卡林福德。”她说着叹了口气，因为她想起了五叶地锦，想起花园那一侧新砌的五英尺墙——为的是挡住火车，才完工不久。生活里没有十全的乐事。可是等摩根太太俯身去拾教区长笨拙的手指从针线盒里碰落的几只散线轴时，眼睛又叫地毯上那些大朵的玫瑰和郁金香吸住了，满足与称意涨满了她的心。
“我也有同感，亲爱的，”摩根先生说。“我不是说菲尼亚尔（Finial）先生作建筑师怎样不好，可那样一座丑教堂，斯科特本人也无能为力。我看文特沃斯不会介意的，”教区长带着一种古怪的自尊感说。此刻他对自己慷慨的举动，感受得几乎同他太太一样深切，禁不住把卡林福德教堂看作一匹送人的马，不便细看牙口。
“不会，”摩根太太说，在这一点上不无一闪而过的疑虑；“他当初若是坦坦荡荡把话说明白，本来什么误会也不会有；不过这一切发生了，我倒高兴，”教区长的太太带着一点热心说。“哦，威廉，我一直这样坏——我一直在想——可如今你是在把炭火堆在他头上了，”她嚷道，喉咙里带着一阵癔症的声音。她自己几乎不明白自己说的是什么，好教区长更没有一丝一毫的懂得——这些都不要紧。

===Original===

She was so glad, that it was almost necessary to be guilty of some extravagance by way of relieving her mind. “After all Mr. Proctor’s care in fitting the furniture, you would not, of course, think of removing it,” said Mrs. Morgan; “Mr. Wentworth will take it as we did; and as for Mrs. Scarsfield, if you like her, William, you may be sure I shall,” the penitent wife said softly, in the flutter and tremor of her agitation. As he saw himself reflected in her eyes, the Rector could not but feel himself a superior person, elevated over other men’s shoulders. Such a sense of goodness promotes the amiability from which it springs. The Rector kissed his wife as he got up from his seat beside her, and once more smoothed down, with a touch which made her feel like a girl again, her pretty brown hair.
“That is all settled satisfactorily,” said Mr. Morgan, “and now I must go to my work again. I thought, if you approved of it, I would write at once to Scarsfield, and also to Buller of All Souls.”
“Do,” said the Rector’s wife﻿—and she too bestowed, in her middle-aged way, a little caress, which was far from being unpleasant to the sober-minded man. He went downstairs in a more agreeable frame of mind than he had known for a long time back. Not that he understood why she had cried about it when he laid his intentions before her. Had Mr. Morgan been a Frenchman, he probably would have imagined his wife’s heart to be touched by the graces of the Perpetual Curate; but, being an Englishman, and rather more certain, on the whole, of her than of himself, it did not occur to him to speculate on the subject. He was quite able to content himself with the thought that women were incomprehensible, as he went back to his study. To be sure, it was best to understand them, if you could; but if not, it did not so very much matter, Mr. Morgan thought; could in this pleasant condition of mind he went downstairs and wrote a little sermon, which ever after was a great favourite, preached upon all special occasions, and always listened to with satisfaction, especially by the Rector’s wife.
When Mrs. Morgan was left alone she sat doing nothing for an entire half-hour, thinking of the strange and unhoped-for change that in a moment had occurred to her.

===Chinese===

她高兴到这个地步，几乎必须干一点出格的事，好舒散她的心。“普罗克特先生布置家具那样经心，那些家具你当然想不到搬走，”摩根太太说；“文特沃斯先生会照我们那样接手；至于斯卡斯菲尔德太太，你若喜欢她，威廉，管保我也喜欢，”这悔罪的太太轻轻说，还处在激动的震颤里。教区长从她的眼睛里照见自己，不能不觉得自己是个高人一头的人物，立在众人的肩上。这样的善自觉，助长它所从出的那份和蔼。教区长从她身旁起身时吻了吻他的太太，又伸手抚平她那头好看的棕发——那一抚，叫她觉得自己又成了个姑娘。
“这样都妥妥帖帖定下了，”摩根先生说，“现在我得回去做工了。我想，你若赞成，我就立刻写信给斯卡斯菲尔德，也给万灵学院的布勒写一封。”
“写吧，”教区长的太太说——她也以她中年人的方式回敬了一点爱抚，对这位持重的男人绝非不愉快。他下楼去时，心境之舒畅是多日来未有的。倒不是他懂得了，为什么他向她摊明心意时她要为这个哭。摩根先生若是法国人，多半会想到是常任副牧师的风采打动了他太太的心；可他是英国人，而且总的来说，他对她的把握还胜过对自己，便根本没往这上头想。他回到书房，尽可以拿“女人是不可解的”这一想自足。当然，能懂她们最好；懂不了，也不很要紧，摩根先生想；他带着这副愉快的心境下了楼，写了一篇小小的讲章——那篇讲章从此成了他的爱宠，逢特别场合必讲，回回听得人称心，尤其是教区长的太太。
摩根太太独自留下，整整半个钟头坐着无所事事，想着那桩一霎间落到她身上的、既古怪又不敢指望的变局。

===Original===

Though she was not young, she had that sense of grievousness, the unbearableness of trouble, which belongs to youth; for, after all, whatever female moralists may say on the subject, the patience of an unmarried woman wearing out her youth in the harassments of a long engagement, is something very different from the hard and many-sided experience of actual life. She had been accustomed for years to think that her troubles would be over when the long-expected event arrived; and when new and more vexatious troubles still sprang up after that event, the woman of one idea was not much better fitted to meet them than if she had been a girl. Now that the momentary cloud had been driven off, Mrs. Morgan’s heart rose more warmly than ever. She changed her mind in a moment about the All Souls pudding, and even added, in her imagination, another dish to the dinner, without pausing to think that *that* also was much approved by Mr. Leeson; and then her thoughts took another turn, and such a vision of a perfect carpet for a drawing-room﻿—something softer and more exquisite than ever came out of mortal loom; full of repose and tranquillity, yet not without seducing beauties of design; a carpet which would never obtrude itself, but yet would catch the eye by dreamy moments in the summer twilight or over the winter fire﻿—flashed upon the imagination of the Rector’s wife. It would be sweet to have a house of one’s own arranging, where everything would be in harmony; and though this sweetness was very secondary to the other satisfaction of having a husband who was not a clay idol, but really deserved his pedestal, it yet supplemented the larger delight, and rounded off all the corners of Mrs. Morgan’s present desires. She wished everybody as happy as herself, in the effusion of the moment, and thought of Lucy Wodehouse, with a little glow of friendliness in which there was still a tincture of admiring envy. All this that happy girl would have without the necessity of waiting for it; but then was it not the Rector, the rehabilitated husband, who would be the means of producing so much happiness? Mrs. Morgan rose up as lightly as a girl when she had reached this stage, and opened her writing-desk, which was one of her wedding-presents, and too fine to be used on common occasions. She took out her prettiest paper, with her monogram in violet, which was her favourite colour.

===Chinese===

她虽不年轻了，却还有那种年轻人独有的、灾祸难当之感；说到底，不论女道德家们在这题目上怎样说，一个闺中女子在漫长婚约的消磨里磨掉青春的耐性，同实际人生那副坚硬的、多棱的阅历相比，究竟两样。她多年来惯于想着：那件久盼的事一到，烦恼便全完了；等那件事过后，新的、更恼人的烦恼仍旧丛生，这位一条心的妇人应付起来，并不比一个姑娘高明多少。此刻一时的阴云驱散了，摩根太太的心比先前任何时节都热。她转念之间就改了主意，万灵学院布丁要做，还在想象里给晚饭另添了一道菜，也不想想*那*一道同样深受利森先生的赏识；随后她的念头又转了个弯，一幅客厅完美地毯的幻象——比人间织机织得出的任何东西更柔和、更精妙；满是安宁静谧，却又自有诱人的花色；一块永不唐突、却又会在夏日黄昏或冬夜炉火边的出神片刻里攫住人眼的地毯——闪过教区长太太的想象。有一所自己作主的宅子该多甜，样样东西都和和谐谐；这份甜虽说远居其次，比不上另一样满足——有一个并非泥胎偶像、真正配得上宝座的丈夫——可它补足了那份更大的欢喜，把摩根太太眼下心愿的各个棱角都磨圆了。在这情不自禁的一刻，她愿人人同她一样幸福，想起了露西·伍德豪斯，心里带着一点亲切的热，其中还掺着一丝艳羡。这一切，那幸福的姑娘不用等待便可得着；可再说，成就这许多福气的，不正是这位教区长——这位重登宝座的丈夫么？摩根太太想到这一步，姑娘似的轻快地站起来，打开了她的写字匣——那是她的嫁妆之一，太贵重，平常舍不得用。她取出她最漂亮的花笺，带着紫罗兰色的花押，那是她心爱的颜色。

===Original===

One of those kind impulses which are born of happiness moved her relieved spirit. To give to another the consolation of a brighter hope, seemed at the moment the most natural way of expressing her own thankful feelings. Instead of going downstairs immediately to order dinner, she sat down instead at the table, and wrote the following note:﻿—

> **My dear Mr. Wentworth**﻿—I don’t know whether you will think me a fair-weather friend seeking you only when everybody else is seeking you, and when you are no longer in want of support and sympathy. Perhaps you will exculpate me when you remember the last conversation we had; but what I write for at present is to ask if you would waive ceremony and come to dinner with us tonight. I am aware that your family are still in Carlingford, and of course I don’t know what engagements you may have; but if you are at liberty, pray come. If Mr. Morgan and you had but known each other a little better things could never have happened which have been a great grief and vexation to me; and I know the Rector *wishes very much* to have a little conversation with you, and has something to speak of in which you would be interested. Perhaps my husband might feel a little strange in asking you to overstep the barrier which somehow has been raised between you two; but I am sure if you knew each other better you would understand each other, and this is one of the things we women ought to be good for. I will take it as a proof that you consider me a friend if you accept my invitation. Our hour is half-past six.﻿—Believe me, very sincerely, yours,
> M. Morgan.

===Chinese===

幸福里生出的一星善念，推动她那释然的心。把一线更明亮的希望送给另一个人，此刻仿佛是表达自家感恩之情最自然的方式。她没有立刻下楼去吩咐晚饭，而是在桌前坐下，写了这样一封短简：

> 亲爱的文特沃斯先生——我不知道你会不会把我看作一个晴天的朋友，只在人人都寻你、你不再需要扶持和同情的时候才来寻你。你想起我们上一次的谈话，或许会替我开脱；可我此刻写信，是想请问你可否抛开客套，今晚来我们这儿吃饭。我知道你家里人还在卡林福德，当然不知道你有什么既定的安排；你若得空，务请过来。摩根先生同你当初只要彼此多了解一点，好些叫我伤心烦恼的事就决不会发生；而且我知道，教区长*非常愿意*同你谈一谈，有件事要对你说，你会感兴趣的。我丈夫请你跨越你们两人中间不知怎么竖起的那道坎，或许会觉得有点唐突；可我深信你们彼此多一分了解，便会多一分懂得，而这正是我们女人应当有用的地方之一。你若接受我的邀请，我就当它看作你拿我当朋友的一个凭据。我们开饭是六点半。——请相信我，你最真诚的，
> M. 摩根

===Original===

When she had written this note Mrs. Morgan went downstairs, stopping at the library door in passing. “I thought I might as well ask Mr. Wentworth to come to us tonight, as we are to have some people to dinner,” she said, looking in at the door. “I thought you might like to talk to him, William; and if his people are going away today, I daresay he will feel rather lonely tonight.” Such was the Jesuitical aspect in which she represented the flag of truce she was sending. Mr. Morgan was a little startled by action so prompt.
“I should like to hear from Buller first,” said the Rector; “he might like to come to Carlingford himself, for anything I can tell; but, to be sure, it can do no harm to have Wentworth to dinner,” said Mr. Morgan, doubtfully; “only Buller, you know, might wish﻿—and in that case it might not be worth our trouble to make any change.”
In spite of herself, Mrs. Morgan’s countenance fell; her pretty scheme of poetic justice, her vision of tasteful and appropriate furniture, became obscured by a momentary mist. “At least it is only right to ask him to dinner,” she said, in subdued tones, and went to speak to the cook in a frame of mind more like the common level of human satisfaction than the exultant and exalted strain to which she had risen at the first moment. Then she put on a black dress, and went to call on the Miss Wodehouses, who naturally came into her mind when she thought of the Perpetual Curate. As she went along Grange Lane she could not but observe a hackney cab, one of those which belong to the railway station, lounging﻿—if a cab could ever be said to lounge﻿—in the direction of Wharfside. Its appearance specially attracted Mrs. Morgan’s attention in consequence of the apparition of Elsworthy’s favourite errand-boy, who now and then poked his head furtively through the window, and seemed to be sitting in state inside. When she had gone a little further she encountered Wodehouse and Jack Wentworth, who had just come from paying their visit to the sisters.

===Chinese===

写完这封短简，摩根太太下了楼，路过书房门口时停了一停。“我们要请几位客人吃饭，我想不妨就请文特沃斯先生今晚来，”她朝门里望了一眼说。“我想你乐得同他谈谈，威廉；他家里的人今天若走，他今晚想必怪冷清的。”这便是她给自己那面休战旗描画出的耶稣会式的面目。摩根先生叫这雷厉风行的举动惊了一下。
“我想先听听布勒的信，”教区长说；“说不定他自己想来卡林福德，我说不准；不过，请文特沃斯吃顿饭当然没有坏处，”摩根先生将信将疑地说；“只是布勒，你知道，说不定愿意——那样的话，劳神动换就不值当了。”
摩根太太不由得神色一黯；她那套诗意的公道的好盘算，她那幅雅致得体的家具的幻象，都蒙上一层一时的雾。“至少请他吃顿饭总是应该的，”她压低了声音说，随后去同厨娘说话，心境已从起初那种扬扬得意的昂扬，落回人间寻常的知足。然后她换上一件黑衣裳，去拜望伍德豪斯家两位小姐——一想起常任副牧师，她们自然就到了她心上。她沿着格兰奇巷走，不能不注意到一辆出租马车——车站上那种——正朝码头区那个方向“闲荡”（倘若马车也能说闲荡的话）。它的模样特别引她注意，因为埃尔斯沃西那位得力的送报小童露了面，不时把头偷偷从车窗里探出来，俨然高坐车里。再走远些，她迎面遇上伍德豪斯同杰克·文特沃斯，他们刚去看过那对姊妹。

===Original===

The sight of these two revived her sympathies for the lonely women who had fallen so unexpectedly out of wealth into poverty; but yet she felt a little difficulty in framing her countenance to be partly sorrowful and partly congratulatory, as was necessary under these circumstances; for though she knew nothing of the accident which had happened that morning, when Lucy and the Perpetual Curate saw each other alone, she was aware of Miss Wodehouse’s special position, and was sympathetic as became a woman who had “gone through” similar experiences. When she had got through her visit and was going home, it struck her with considerable surprise to see the cab still lingering about the corner of Prickett’s Lane. Was Elsworthy’s pet boy delivering his newspapers from that dignified elevation? or were they seizing the opportunity of conveying away the unfortunate little girl who had caused so much annoyance to everybody? When she went closer, with a little natural curiosity to see what else might be inside besides the furtive errand-boy, the cab made a little rush away from her, and the blinds were drawn down. Mrs. Morgan smiled a little to herself with dignified calm. “As if it was anything to me!” she said to herself; and so went home to put out the dessert with her own hands. She even cut a few fronds of her favourite maidenhair to decorate the peaches, of which she could not help being a little proud. “I must speak to Mr. Wentworth, if he comes, to keep on Thompson,” she said to herself, and then gave a momentary sigh at the thought of the new flue, which was as good as her own invention, and which it had cost her both time and money to arrange to her satisfaction. The peaches were lovely, but who could tell what they might be next year if a new Rector came who took no interest in the garden?﻿—for Thompson, though he was a very good servant, required to be looked after, as indeed most good servants do. Mrs. Morgan sighed a little when she thought of all her past exertions and the pains, of which she was scarcely yet beginning to reap the fruit. One man labours, and another enters into his labours. One thing, however, was a little consolatory, that she could take her ferns with her. But on the whole, after the first outburst of feeling, the idea of change, notwithstanding all its advantages, was in itself, like most human things, a doubtful pleasure.

===Chinese===

这两个人一入眼，她对那两位从富贵意外跌进贫寒的孤女又生同情；可她觉得，要把面容调配得一半悲悯、一半道贺——这种场合原该如此——倒有一点费事；因为她虽不知道那天早晨露西同常任副牧师单独相见出了什么事，却知道伍德豪斯小姐眼下的特殊地位，也带着一个“经过”类似事变的妇人应有的同情。拜访完毕往回走，她相当吃惊地看见那辆马车还在普里基特巷口徘徊。是埃尔斯沃西的心肝小童坐在那尊严的高座上送他的报纸？还是他们正趁便把那个给众人添了这许多烦恼的倒霉小姑娘运走？她怀着一点自然的好奇走近，想看看那鬼鬼祟祟的送报童之外车里还坐着谁，马车猛地往前一蹿，躲开她，遮帘也放了下来。摩根太太端庄地对自己微微一笑。“好像与我相干似的！”她自语道；就这样回家，亲手去摆果碟。她甚至剪了几枝心爱的铁线蕨，来衬那几只桃子——那几只桃子，她不由得有点得意。“文特沃斯先生若来，我得同他说一声，把汤普森（Thompson）留下来，”她自忖道；随即想起那条新砌的暖房烟道，又一时叹息——那烟道简直是她自己的发明，为叫它称心，费了她多少工夫和钱。桃子是可爱的；可新教区长若来了一位不着意花园的，明年它们会怎样，谁说得准？——汤普森虽是个很好的仆人，也少不了人看管，其实大多数好仆人都这样。摩根太太想起自己过去的这一切操劳、这一切辛苦——收成才刚开始尝到一点——不由叹了口气。一人撒种，另一人收割。不过有一点还算安慰：她的蕨草可以随身带走。可总的说来，情感初潮过后，搬家这个主意——纵有百般好处——本身也同人间大多数事物一样，是一桩掺疑的乐事。

===Original===

To be sure, it was only through its products that her feelings were interested about the new flue, whereas the drawing-room carpet was a standing grievance. When it was time to dress for dinner, the Rector’s wife was not nearly so sure as before that she had never liked Carlingford. She began to forget the thoughts she had entertained about broken idols, and to remember a number of inconveniences attending a removal. Who would guarantee the safe transit of the china, not to speak of the *old* china, which was one of the most valuable decorations of the Rectory? This kind of breakage, if not more real, was at least likely to force itself more upon the senses than the other kind of fracture which this morning’s explanation had happily averted; and altogether it was with mingled feelings that Mrs. Morgan entered the drawing-room, and found it occupied by Mr. Leeson, who always came too early, and who, on the present occasion, had some sufficiently strange news to tell.

===Chinese===

的确，新烟道牵动她感情的，不过是它的产物；客厅地毯却是常年的心病。到了换装吃饭的时辰，教区长的太太对于“自己从来不曾喜欢过卡林福德”这话，远不似先前那样有把握了。她开始忘掉那些破偶像的念头，记起搬家的一连串不便。谁能保瓷器平安过户，更不必说那批*老*瓷器——那是教区长宅最贵重的陈设之一？这种碎裂，纵然不见得比今天早晨那场解释所幸而避免的另一种破裂更实，至少更容易强闯进人的感官；总之，摩根太太带着一身混杂的心绪走进客厅，发现利森先生已坐在里面——他总是来得太早——而这一次，他带来的新闻也够奇怪了。

## XLVI / 四十六
===Original===

Mr. Wentworth did not accept Mrs. Morgan’s sudden invitation, partly because his “people” did not leave Carlingford that evening, and partly because, though quite amiably disposed towards the Rector, whom he had worsted in fair fight, he was not sufficiently interested in anything he was likely to hear or see in Mr. Morgan’s house to move him to spend his evening there. He returned a very civil answer to the invitation of the Rector’s wife, thanking her warmly for her friendliness, and explaining that he could not leave his father on the last night of his stay in Carlingford; after which he went to dinner at his aunts’, where the household was still much agitated. Not to speak of all the events which had happened and were happening, Jack, who had begun to tire of his new character of the repentant prodigal, had shown himself in a new light that evening, and was preparing to leave, to the relief of all parties. The prodigal, who no longer pretended to be penitent, had taken the conversation into his own hands at dinner. “I have had things my own way since I came here,” said Jack; “somehow it appears I have a great luck for having things my own way. It is you scrupulous people who think of others and of such antiquated stuff as duty, and so forth, that get yourselves into difficulties. My dear aunt, I am going away; if I were to remain an inmate of this house﻿—I mean to say, could I look forward to the privilege of continuing a member of this Christian family﻿—another day, I should know better how to conduct myself; but I am going back to my bad courses, aunt Dora; I am returning to the world﻿—”
“Oh! Jack, my dear, I hope not,” said aunt Dora, who was much bewildered, and did not know what to say.
“Too true,” said the relapsed sinner; “and considering all the lessons you have taught me, don’t you think it is the best thing I could do? There is my brother Frank, who has been carrying other people about on his shoulders, and doing his duty; but I don’t see that you good people are at all moved in his behalf. You leave him to fight his way by himself, and confer your benefits elsewhere, which is an odd sort of lesson for a worldling like me. As for Gerald, you know he’s a virtuous fool, as I have heard you all declare. There is nothing in the world that I can see to prevent him keeping his living and doing as he pleases, as most parsons do.

===Chinese===

文特沃斯先生没有接受摩根太太这突如其来的邀请，一来他的“家里人”当晚并不离开卡林福德，二来他虽对那位公平较量中被他击败的教区长毫无恶意，却对摩根先生家里可能听到、看到的任何东西都提不起兴致，不值得为它搭上一个晚上。他给教区长的妻子回了封十分客气的信，热诚感谢她的好意，说明父亲在卡林福德的最后一晚，他不能撇下他；随后便到姑妈家吃饭去——那一家人仍旧激动得很。且不说已经发生、正在发生的种种大事，杰克——他已开始厌倦悔罪浪子这个新角色——当晚又露了一手新面目，正准备走，叫各个方面都松了口气。这位不再装悔罪的浪子，吃饭时把话头抢到了自己手里。“我来到这儿以后，事事都如了我的意，”杰克说；“不知怎么，我在自行其在这上头运气好得很。倒是你们这些有忌讳的人，心里想着别人，想着本分之类的老古董，才把自己弄进难处。亲爱的姑妈，我要走了；我若继续做这家里的一员——我是说，我若能指望再享受一天这份做基督化家庭成员的特权——我该怎么举止，倒会更有数些；可我要回到我的老路上去了，多拉姑妈；我要回到世上——”
“哦！杰克，亲爱的，我盼着不是这样，”多拉姑妈说，她糊涂极了，不知说什么好。
“千真万确，”这重堕的罪人说；“想想你们教给我的这些功课，你们不觉得这正是我最好的出路吗？瞧我弟弟弗兰克，把别人扛在肩上，尽他的本分；我可没见你们这些好人为他动过一点心。你们由他一个人去闯，把恩典另行赏人——对我这样的俗人，这可是个古怪的教益。至于杰拉尔德，你们都知道他是个有德的傻子，这话我听你们人人说过。我看天下没有什么拦着他，尽可以像多数牧师那样，守着俸禄，爱怎么便怎么。

===Original===

However, that’s his own business. It is Frank’s case which is the edifying case to me. If my convictions of sin had gone just a step farther,” said the pitiless critic, “if I had devoted myself to bringing others to repentance, as is the first duty of a reformed sinner, my aunt Leonora would not have hesitated to give Skelmersdale to me﻿—”
“Jack, hold your tongue,” said Miss Leonora; but though her cheeks burned, her voice was not so firm as usual, and she actually failed in putting down the man who had determined to have his say.
“Fact, my dear aunt,” said Jack; “if I had been a greater rascal than I am, and gone a little farther, you and your people would have thought me quite fit for a cure of souls. I’d have come in for your good things that way as well as other ways; but here is Frank, who even I can see is a right sort of parson. I don’t pretend to fixed theological opinions,” said this unlooked-for oracle, with a comic glance aside at Gerald, the most unlikely person present to make any response; “but, so far as I can see, he’s a kind of fellow most men would be glad to make a friend of when they were under a cloud﻿—not that he was ever very civil to me. I tell you, so far from rewarding him for being of the true sort, you do nothing but snub him, that I can see. He looks to me as good for work as any man I know; but you’ll give your livings to any kind of wretched make-believe before you’ll give them to Frank. I am aware,” said the heir of the Wentworths, with a momentary flush, “that I have never been considered much of a credit to the family; but if I were to announce my intention of marrying and settling, there is not one of the name that would not lend a hand to smooth matters. That is the reward of wickedness,” said Jack, with a laugh; “as for Frank, he’s a perpetual curate, and may marry perhaps fifty years hence; that’s the way you good people treat a man who never did anything to be ashamed of in his life; and you expect me to give up my evil courses after such a lesson? I trust I am not such a fool,” said the relapsed prodigal. He sat looking at them all in his easy way, enjoying the confusion, the indignation, and wrath with which his address was received. “The man who gets his own way is the man who takes it,” he concluded, with his usual composure, pouring out Miss Leonora’s glass of claret as he spoke.

===Chinese===

不过那是他自己的事。弗兰克的案子才是给我教益的案子。我那知罪之心若再往前走一步，”这位不留情面的批评家说，“我若献身去劝人悔改——那是悔改罪人的第一本分——我莱奥诺拉姑妈准会毫不迟疑把斯凯尔默斯代尔给我——”
“杰克，住嘴，”莱奥诺拉小姐说；可她尽管两颊发烧，嗓音却不似平常坚定，那个打定主意要说话的人，她竟没能压下去。
“实情，亲爱的姑妈，”杰克说；“我若比现在更无赖一点，再往前走一小步，你们和你们那一伙准会认为我十分配牧养灵魂。你们的好东西，我原也可以从那条路上得一份，同别的路一样；可弗兰克呢，连我都看得出他是个正经牧师。我不冒充有什么固定的神学见解，”这位不期而至的先知说，滑稽地瞟了一眼杰拉尔德——在场的人里最不可能答腔的一个；“可依我看，他是那种男人倒了霉人人都乐意结交的朋友——虽说他对我也算不得多客气。我告诉你们，你们非但不酬报他是正经人，据我看，你们只会挫他。我看他干活的本事不输我认识的任何人；可你们宁可把俸禄给随便哪个蹩脚的冒牌货，也不给弗兰克。我知道，”温特沃斯家的嗣子说，脸上掠过一阵红，“家里从来不把我当多大的体面；可我若宣布我要成家立业，姓这个姓的没有一个不会伸手把事情抹平。这就是恶行的报偿，”杰克笑道；“至于弗兰克，他是个常驻副牧师，兴许五十年后才娶得上妻；这就是你们这些好人对待一个生平没做过一件亏心事的人的办法；吃了这一课，还要我改邪归正？我信得自己不是那样的傻子，”这重堕的浪子说。他懒散地坐在那里，望着他们大家，享受他这番话引起的慌乱、愤慨与恼怒。“自行其是的人，就是把它夺到手的人，”他总结道，神色如常，一面给莱奥诺拉小姐的杯子斟上红葡萄酒。

===Original===

Nobody had ever before seen the strong-minded woman in so much agitation. “Frank knows what my feelings are,” she said, abruptly. “I have a great respect for himself, but I have no confidence in his principles. I﻿—I have explained my ideas about Church patronage﻿—”
But here the Squire broke in. “I always said, sir,” said the old man, with an unsteady voice, “that if I ever lived to see a thing or two amended that was undoubtedly objectionable, your brother Jack’s advice would be invaluable to the family as a﻿—as a man of the world. I have nothing to say against clergymen, sir,” continued the Squire, without it being apparent whom he was addressing, “but I have always expressed my conviction of﻿—of the value of your brother Jack’s advice as﻿—as a man of the world.”
This speech had a wonderful effect upon the assembled family, but most of all upon the son thus commended, who lost all his ease and composure as his father spoke, and turned his head stiffly to one side, as if afraid to meet the Squire’s eyes, which indeed were not seeking his, but were fixed upon the table, as was natural, considering the state of emotion in which Mr. Wentworth was. As for Jack, when he had steadied himself a little, he got up from his seat and tried to laugh, though the effort was far from being a successful one.
“Even my father applauds me, you see, because I am a scamp and don’t deserve it,” he said, with a voice which was partially choked. “Goodbye, sir; I am going away.”
The Squire rose too, with the hazy bewildered look of which his other children were afraid.
“Goodbye, sir,” said the old man, and then made a pause before he held out his hand. “You’ll not forget what I’ve said, Jack,” he added, with a little haste. “It’s true enough, though I haven’t that confidence in you that﻿—that I might have had. I am getting old, and I have had two attacks, sir,” said Mr. Wentworth, with dignity; “and anyhow, I can’t live forever. Your brothers can make their own way in the world, but I haven’t saved all that I could have wished. When I am gone, Jack, be just to the girls and the little children,” said the Squire; and with that took his son’s hand and grasped it hard, and looked his heir full in the face.
Jack Wentworth was not prepared for any such appeal; he was still less prepared to discover the unexpected and inevitable sequence with which one good sentiment leads to another.

谁也不曾见过这位意志坚强的女人这样激动。“弗兰克知道我的心意，”她生硬地说。“我敬重他本人，可我不信任他的原则。我——我把我对教会圣职委任的主张解释过——”
